title: A gauge-invariant theory of small Markovian errors in quantum gate sets
authors: Juan Gonzalez De Mendoza, Corey Ostrove, Timothy Proctor, Kevin Young, Erik Nielsen, Robin Blume-Kohout
abstract: Noisy logic operations on a quantum computational register -- e.g., one or more qubits -- can be described by transfer matrices (a.k.a. CPTP maps or superoperators) that act linearly on the density matrix representing the register's quantum state. Collectively, these operations form a gate set. Gate sets have a gauge freedom; many gate sets that appear different actually predict the same experimental outcomes. A property of a gate set can be observable (and thus physically relevant) only if it is gauge-invariant. Unfortunately, no good gauge-invariant parameterizations of gate sets are known. We introduce the next best thing, a perturbative gauge-invariant parameterization of small Markovian errors in gate sets. We construct vector spaces of properties that are first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI). We show how to construct and understand FOGI properties, how to use them as coordinates to parameterize gate sets without gauge freedom, and how to extract approximately gauge-invariant error metrics.
summary: This paper tackles the ambiguity arising from gauge freedom when describing noisy quantum gates. It introduces First-Order Gauge-Invariant (FOGI) properties as a systematic, physically relevant way to parameterize small errors in gate sets. This provides essential tools for developing robust and unambiguous error characterization metrics for quantum computing hardware.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing a physically meaningful, gauge-invariant way to characterize small errors in quantum gate sets.
main_result: The authors introduce First-Order Gauge-Invariant (FOGI) properties that provide coordinates for parameterizing gate sets without suffering from unphysical gauge ambiguities. They derive systematic methods to construct these basis elements.
method: The approach involves linearizing the error structure around a target gate set and identifying properties whose first-order deviation is insensitive to small gauge transformations, leading to kernel calculations on gauge action matrices.
model_or_system: The system models quantum computation using qubits, where operations are represented by superoperators (transfer matrices) acting on density matrices. The structure includes an initial state preparation, a sequence of logic gates, and a final measurement.
key_observables: Gauge-invariant error metrics derived from FOGI properties; the dimension of the intrinsic FOGI space ($	ext{FG}$).
important_parameters: The small error parameter $\epsilon$, which governs the linearization approximation ($O(\epsilon)$ vs $O(\epsilon^2)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on assuming that errors are small (perturbative) and that the gate set is informationally complete (IC) for certain key theorems.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the structure of a general 1-qubit gate set. Figure 8(d) shows the collection of 19 FOGI properties forming a basis for $	ext{FG}_7$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically defines gauge freedom in quantum operations, introduces the concept of FOGI properties to quantify observable errors, and develops computational procedures using kernel analysis on gauge action matrices to construct bases for these invariant error spaces.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous mathematical framework for defining 'physical' error metrics in quantum computation that are independent of arbitrary choices (gauge fixing), which is crucial for comparing experimental results across different hardware platforms.
